thesis: The $4 gasoline that Walmart blamed for its 2.6% comp miss is the same input that routes low-income grocery spend into dollar stores, and DG has already de-rated 23.8% from its 158.23 high while the trade-down it should capture is only now arriving. exit.scale_plan: no trim until gold takes out the prior high; this is a core holding, not a trade

catalyst.event: Fiscal dominance: the Treasury doubled its long-bond buyback to $4B (effective Sep 9-Nov 4) and the 30y still made a two-decade high at 5.249% the next session, while Bessent publicly pressures Warsh Fed to ease. Central banks absorbing ~755 tonnes/yr as price-insensitive buyers.
catalyst.action: Accumulate in thirds: first tranche near 398, second under 390, third under 380. No urgency - the driver is measured in years and the entry is a pullback, not a breakout.

thesis: When the sovereign issuer doubles its own bond buyback and the long end sells off anyway, the marginal buyer of duration is gone and the debasement bid is the residual - that is precisely the 2026 tape, with the deficit set to exceed 2025, inflation persistently above target and corporate issuance crowding Treasurys. Gold is 18.5% below its 509.70 high after a positioning washout and is only now reclaiming its 200-day (413.21) from below, so the structural thesis is intact while the price still carries correction damage. Central banks bought ~755t and, unlike ETFs, do not sell on bad days.
key_risk: Gold is a real-rate asset and the 10y is at 4.70%. If the long-end selloff turns out to be a growth/term-premium story that ends with the Fed staying restrictive and real yields grinding higher, gold falls with bonds rather than hedging them - the January silver washout showed how violently this complex unwinds when leveraged longs are forced out. Invalidation: central bank net purchases turning negative for two consecutive quarters, or gold closing below 361.39 (the correction low, ~$3,890/oz), which would say the debasement bid has failed on its own terms.
counter_argument: The banks that ran gold up are marking it down: Goldman cut its end-2026 target from $5,400 to $4,900, JPMorgan to $4,500 for Q4, HSBC to $4,560 - all clustered at or barely above the current $4,475 spot. On the sell side consensus, gold is roughly fairly valued and my 520 target requires the very forecasters who own this call to be too conservative. Gold has also already rallied 15% off 361.39, so much of the easy repair is done.

thesis: This is a position-management update, not a fresh pitch. Boise Cascade is wood products into new residential construction and the 30y at 5.249% is a direct headwind, so the original 76.00 stop - 7% and nearly 2 ATR away - gave too much room to a thesis the macro is now arguing against. The reason to hold rather than exit, unlike HD, is that BCC structure is still intact: it sits on its 20-day at 81.99 and above both the 50-day (77.69) and 200-day (76.58), and builders with rate-buydown budgets are far less rate-elastic than the existing-home turnover HD depends on.
key_risk: The same rate move that is closing HD can take BCC down with it regardless of the builder-vs-resale distinction - lumber demand is lumber demand. Liquidity is thin at $27.7M average daily dollar volume, so a fast move gaps rather than trades, and the 76.90 stop sits in a crowded zone right below the 50-day where stop runs are common.
counter_argument: Splitting hairs between builder demand and resale turnover is a rationalisation for not taking the same exit I am taking in HD and LCII. If the honest read is that the whole rate-sensitive housing complex is uninvestable while the long end makes two-decade highs, then BCC should be closed too, and the only real argument for keeping it is that it is the one that has not broken yet.

catalyst.action: enter half before the speech, add the second half only after it; do not put full size on ahead of an unpriceable debut

thesis: The dollar index is at 98.558, its lowest since May 14, and it is falling for the specific reason that helps emerging markets most - foreign capital demanding term premium to hold US debt rather than the Fed tightening - while flows into the two largest EM equity ETFs run at their strongest in over a decade. EEM is the one major EM vehicle with both room and structure: 6.92% below its 71.57 high with the price above its 200-day at 61.07, where VWO has only 2.4% of room and FXI and EWZ are both still below their 200-days.
key_risk: The entire thesis is one variable - the dollar - and one man reprices it on Aug 28. Warsh has a hawkish record and no Jackson Hole track record as chair, so a firm debut asserting Fed independence against Bessent public pressure would bounce DXY off a three-month low and take EM down hard through the 63.00 stop in a session. EEM is also a basket, so it dilutes any single-country catalyst into beta.
counter_argument: EEM sits exactly on its 50-day at 66.04 having gone nowhere for two months, which says the record inflows are being absorbed by supply rather than driving price - flows are a coincident indicator, not a leading one. And buying EM because the US long end is broken assumes contagion runs one way; historically a genuine US term-premium shock takes emerging markets down harder than the US, not less.

catalyst.event: Latin American digital-payments conversion compounding at mid-teens, with a $150M buyback (raised from ~$83M remaining on Jul 31, 2026) retiring 8.4% of the company and a falling dollar translating LatAm revenue into more USD.
catalyst.action: Accumulate in halves near 29.40 and on any retest of the 200-day at 28.28. No urgency and no chasing above 30.20 - the buyback is the patient bid underneath.

thesis: Five distinct insiders made seven open-market purchases totalling $2.25M between May 8 and Jun 12 against just $1.4M of sales - a genuine cluster of independent decisions, not one director topping up - and the stock still trades below where several of them bought. The business behind that vote is compounding fast and priced as if it is not: Q2 revenue rose 20% to $274.8M on Latin America, adjusted EBITDA rose 18% to $109.3M, adjusted EPS rose 18% to $1.05, and management raised FY26 guidance to $1.085-1.095B revenue and $3.94-4.04 adjusted EPS - yet the forward P/E is 7.15 on a $1.78B market cap trading $12.4M a day. A mid-teens grower in payments at 7x forward earnings, buying back 8.4% of itself, is a valuation gap that does not need a catalyst to close.
key_risk: This is a $1.78B company trading $12.4M a day with a 4.51% ATR, so a 2% position is a meaningful share of daily volume and must be built with limit orders over days, not bought in one clip. The concentration risk is geographic and currency: revenue is Puerto Rico plus Latin America, so a LatAm FX crisis or a Puerto Rico fiscal or contract shock hits revenue and translation at once - the same weak-dollar tailwind reverses violently if the dollar rallies. GAAP net income fell to $5.41M even as adjusted EBITDA rose 18%, so the gap between adjusted and reported earnings is wide and must be watched. Invalidation: adjusted EBITDA margin falling for two consecutive quarters, or the buyback being suspended.
counter_argument: A 7x forward multiple on a 17% grower is not a gift, it is the market pricing the adjusted numbers as fiction - GAAP net income of $5.41M against $109.3M of adjusted EBITDA is a very large reconciliation, and if the amortisation and one-off charges bridging them are actually recurring costs of doing business then the real multiple is the 19.19 trailing P/E, not 7.15, and the stock is roughly fairly valued. The insider cluster also stopped in June, well before the July 31 buyback expansion.

entry.condition: Accumulate in thirds: 276, 262 (the 50-day), and 240 on any capitulation toward the 228.63 low. Do not commit full size before the mid-Atlantic rate-cap proposal has a defined shape.

exit.scale_plan: trim a third at 340; hold the balance toward the 384.98 prior high, which the business is now better positioned to justify than when it traded there

catalyst.event: US grid scarcity repricing: PJM capacity cleared at $329.17/MW-day for 2026/27 versus $28.92 for 2024/25, and the 2027/28 auction failed to procure enough supply for the first time in PJM history. PJM plans a reliability backstop procurement auction in Autumn 2026.
catalyst.action: Accumulate in thirds on weakness over the next two quarters. The driver runs to 2030; there is no reason to pay up for a single entry.

thesis: The physical fact and the share price are pointing in opposite directions, which is the whole idea. PJM capacity prices went from $28.92 to $329.17 per MW-day in two delivery years - more than tenfold - and the 2027/28 auction failed to secure enough supply for the first time ever, with data centers set to add over 30GW of peak demand by 2030. Constellation owns the nuclear baseload that hyperscalers specifically need for 24/7 carbon-free power, yet it trades 29.1% below its high, having been de-rated on political headlines rather than on power economics. One director bought $417,931 on the open market and there have been zero insider sales in six months.
key_risk: The de-rating is not irrational and the political risk is concrete, not hypothetical: the Trump Administration and mid-Atlantic governors have floated capping electricity rates in exactly the region where these assets sit, and New York has a one-year moratorium on environmental permits for large data centers. A rate cap converts a scarcity windfall into a regulated return and would break this thesis outright. Management also guided 2026 adjusted earnings below consensus and is still digesting the Calpine acquisition, so the earnings bridge to a 385 share price is not yet visible. Invalidation: mid-Atlantic rate caps being enacted in law, or PJM capacity clearing materially lower in the Autumn 2026 backstop auction.
counter_argument: The market has seen the same PJM numbers I have and sold the stock anyway, which is usually a sign the constraint is not the scarcity but who is allowed to collect on it. Political backlash tends to arrive precisely when a windfall becomes large and visible enough to be worth legislating against - so the very datapoint I am calling the bull case ($329/MW-day) is what makes a rate cap likely. The stock hit a 52-week low and drew a Citi downgrade; buying an AI-power darling that has already lost 35% of its value in the first half on the argument that it is cheap assumes the de-rating is finished, and nothing in the tape says that yet.
